title: Serval raises $150M at $3B to replace ServiceNow with AI agents
subtitle: Sequoia led the Series C, Serval's third round in 12 months, as its IT-support agents expand into HR, finance, and legal workflows.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: On October 29, San Francisco-based Serval announced a $150 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation, led by Sequoia. It is the company's third round in twelve months — roughly triple the $1 billion valuation it hit in December when it raised $75 million. Existing investors Elad Gil, Evantic, First Round, General Catalyst, and Redpoint joined, with Conviction and Headline coming in as new backers. Serval said it plans to hire more than 500 people, including over 100 engineers it will embed with customers.

Serval sells AI agents for employee support. It started inside IT — managing staff access, troubleshooting hardware and software, provisioning accounts — the kind of work ticketed through ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, or Zendesk. The company says customers have pulled those agents into HR, finance, and legal workflows on their own, which is why this round is pitched as an expansion beyond IT. Reporting positions the company explicitly as a ServiceNow challenger, in a market where incumbents charge seat-license revenue to do work that an agent now does per-ticket.

This is one of the sharper examples of the agentic-enterprise thesis actually translating into revenue and valuation. Service management is a $20 billion-plus category dominated by one incumbent whose UI was designed for humans filing forms; Serval is pricing against work completed, not users seated. The pattern — reasonable-size SaaS category, incumbent with high switching costs, agentic-first entrant pricing on outcomes — is the one investors keep looking for and rarely find. Whether Serval is the one that wins is a different question; what matters is that the model is now funded at a real valuation.

A takeaway for learners: when you hear 'AI agents will replace SaaS,' this is what that looks like concretely. Not a chatbot bolted onto an existing product, but a different purchasing unit — pay per resolved ticket rather than per seat — that forces incumbents to defend margin instead of just launching an AI copilot. For an engineer or an operator, the useful question is not 'is my job going away' but 'which workflows in my company look like IT tickets': structured input, structured output, clear success criteria. Those are the first ones agents touch, and they tell you where to focus.
